meta.title: Danish Driving Theory Test - Original Question Bank
meta.note: Original content authored from public Danish traffic rules (Færdselsloven) and Færdselsstyrelsen test structure. No third-party question content reused. Images/illustrations to be sourced separately (own or licensed).

questions.scenario: You approach an unmarked intersection with no signs, signals, or road markings. A car is approaching from your right at the same time.

subquestions.text: You must give way to the car on your right.
subquestions.explanation: At unmarked intersections the right-hand rule (højrevigepligt) applies — yield to traffic from your right.

subquestions.text: You may proceed if you arrive at the intersection slightly first.
subquestions.explanation: Arrival order does not override the right-hand rule at unmarked intersections.

questions.scenario: You are exiting a roundabout. A cyclist is riding in the cycle lane around the roundabout and will cross your exit path.

subquestions.text: You must give way to the cyclist before exiting.
subquestions.explanation: Cyclists continuing around a roundabout have priority over vehicles exiting across the cycle lane.

subquestions.text: Cyclists must always give way to cars inside a roundabout.
subquestions.explanation: Yield direction depends on movement; a car exiting across a continuing cyclist's path must yield.

questions.scenario: You are turning left at a junction with oncoming traffic and no traffic signal.

subquestions.text: You must give way to oncoming traffic going straight or turning right.
subquestions.explanation: A left turn yields to oncoming through-traffic and right-turning traffic.

subquestions.text: You may turn left first if your indicator was on earlier.
subquestions.explanation: Signaling does not grant priority; movement determines right of way.

questions.scenario: A pedestrian is standing at the edge of a marked pedestrian crossing (fodgængerfelt) without traffic lights, showing intent to cross.

subquestions.text: You must stop or slow down to let the pedestrian cross.
subquestions.explanation: Vehicles give way to pedestrians at unsignalled marked crossings once intent is clear.

subquestions.text: You only need to give way once the pedestrian has stepped into the road.
subquestions.explanation: Give way as soon as intent is clear, not after they enter the roadway.

questions.scenario: You are on a road marked with a 'unbroken give-way line' (hajtænder / shark teeth) approaching a larger road.

subquestions.text: You must give way to all traffic on the larger road.
subquestions.explanation: Shark-teeth markings and the give-way triangle mean you yield to crossing traffic.

subquestions.text: You may enter as long as you signal.
subquestions.explanation: Give-way obligation stands regardless of signaling.

questions.scenario: You are on a road with a give-way sign (the inverted triangle) approaching a main road.

subquestions.text: You must yield to traffic on the main road but need not stop if it is clear.
subquestions.explanation: A give-way sign requires yielding, not a full stop if the way is clear.

subquestions.text: A give-way sign has the same meaning as a stop sign.
subquestions.explanation: A stop sign requires a complete stop; a give-way sign does not if the road is clear.

questions.scenario: You reach a red octagonal stop sign at a junction with clear visibility and no other traffic.

subquestions.text: You must come to a complete stop even if the road is clear.
subquestions.explanation: A stop sign always requires a full stop, regardless of visibility.

questions.scenario: An emergency vehicle approaches from behind with lights and sirens active while you are at a junction.

subquestions.text: You must make way, pulling over safely where possible.
subquestions.explanation: Drivers must give way to emergency vehicles under blue lights and sirens.

subquestions.text: You should stop immediately in the middle of the junction.
subquestions.explanation: Clear the junction first, then pull over safely — stopping in the junction blocks the emergency vehicle.

questions.scenario: You are leaving a private driveway or car park onto a public road.

subquestions.text: You must give way to all traffic and pedestrians on the road you are joining.
subquestions.explanation: Traffic emerging from private ground yields to all road users.

questions.scenario: Traffic lights at a junction are out of order (not lit at all).

subquestions.text: You should treat the junction with caution and apply the normal right of way rules.
subquestions.explanation: With dead signals, fall back to signs/markings or the right-hand rule and proceed carefully.

subquestions.text: You always have priority when lights are off.
subquestions.explanation: No one has automatic priority; normal rules and caution apply.

questions.scenario: You are on a road marked as a priority road (yellow diamond sign) approaching a side road.

subquestions.text: Traffic entering from the side road must give way to you.
subquestions.explanation: The yellow diamond marks a priority road; entering traffic yields to you.

subquestions.text: You must still slow and give way to the side road.
subquestions.explanation: On a priority road you keep priority; you need not yield to the side road.

questions.scenario: Two cars reach a narrow bridge from opposite directions; a sign shows a red arrow and a black arrow indicating priority.

subquestions.text: The sign tells you who must give way at the narrowing.
subquestions.explanation: Priority-over-oncoming and give-way-to-oncoming signs govern narrow sections.

questions.scenario: You are turning at a green light but pedestrians have a green walk signal to cross the road you're turning into.

subquestions.text: You must give way to the crossing pedestrians before completing your turn.
subquestions.explanation: A green light for you does not override pedestrians crossing on their own green.

questions.scenario: A bus is signalling to pull out from a bus stop in a built-up area.

subquestions.text: You should let the bus pull out if you can do so safely.
subquestions.explanation: In town, drivers must give way to buses signalling to leave a stop where safe.

subquestions.text: The bus must always wait for all cars to pass first.
subquestions.explanation: In built-up areas the bus has priority to rejoin traffic when signalling.

questions.scenario: You approach a junction controlled by a police officer directing traffic, while the traffic light shows green for you.

subquestions.text: You must obey the police officer's signals over the traffic light.
subquestions.explanation: Directions from a police officer override traffic signals.

questions.scenario: You approach a roundabout and traffic is already circulating.

subquestions.text: You must give way to traffic already in the roundabout.
subquestions.explanation: Entering traffic yields to vehicles already circulating.

subquestions.text: You have priority because you are entering.
subquestions.explanation: Circulating traffic has priority over entering traffic.

questions.scenario: You want to make a U-turn on a normal road.

subquestions.text: You must give way to all other traffic while turning.
subquestions.explanation: A U-turn yields to oncoming and passing traffic.

questions.scenario: You are reversing out of a parking space onto a road.

subquestions.text: You must give way to traffic and pedestrians already on the road.
subquestions.explanation: Reversing drivers yield to existing road users.

questions.scenario: Two vehicles meet on a narrow road where only one can pass and there is a passing place on your side.

subquestions.text: You should use the passing place to let the other vehicle through.
subquestions.explanation: Whoever is nearer a passing place typically uses it to allow passage.

questions.scenario: You are driving in a built-up area (byzone) with no posted speed limit signs.

subquestions.text: The default speed limit is 50 km/h.
subquestions.explanation: Inside built-up areas the default without signage is 50 km/h.

subquestions.text: You may drive up to 60 km/h if the road is empty.
subquestions.explanation: The default applies regardless of traffic level.

questions.scenario: You are on a rural road (landevej) with no posted signs, in wet conditions.

subquestions.text: The default is 80 km/h, but you must reduce speed for wet conditions.
subquestions.explanation: 80 km/h is the rural default; drivers must adjust to conditions like rain or poor visibility.

subquestions.text: You must always drive at the default limit regardless of conditions.
subquestions.explanation: The limit is a maximum, not a target.

questions.scenario: You are driving on a motorway (motorvej) with no posted signs.

subquestions.text: The default motorway limit for cars is 130 km/h.
subquestions.explanation: Default motorway limit is 130 km/h unless posted otherwise.

subquestions.text: The same default applies to a car towing a trailer.
subquestions.explanation: Cars with trailers have a lower maximum (typically 80 km/h).

questions.scenario: You approach a warning sign showing children, near a school, with no numeric speed sign.

subquestions.text: You should reduce speed and be prepared to stop.
subquestions.explanation: Warning signs for children require increased caution regardless of a posted number.

questions.scenario: You enter a zone marked with a sign showing '30' inside a red circle.

subquestions.text: The maximum speed in this zone is 30 km/h.
subquestions.explanation: A number in a red circle sets the maximum permitted speed.

questions.scenario: You are towing a trailer on a rural road with a car.

subquestions.text: A lower speed limit generally applies when towing a trailer.
subquestions.explanation: Vehicles with trailers have reduced maximum speeds compared to solo cars.

questions.scenario: You are driving in heavy fog with visibility under 50 metres.

subquestions.text: You must reduce speed so you can stop within the distance you can see.
subquestions.explanation: Speed must always allow stopping within visible clear distance.

subquestions.text: You can keep the normal limit as long as your fog lights are on.
subquestions.explanation: Lights help visibility but do not remove the duty to slow for conditions.

questions.scenario: You leave a built-up area and pass the sign marking the end of the town zone.

subquestions.text: The default speed limit increases to the rural default unless otherwise posted.
subquestions.explanation: Leaving byzone raises the default to the outside-town limit (80 km/h) unless signs say otherwise.

questions.scenario: You enter a 'living street' / play street (opholds- og legeområde) marked with the blue sign.

subquestions.text: You must drive at walking pace and give way to people using the street.
subquestions.explanation: On a play street you drive at walking pace and yield to pedestrians and children.

questions.scenario: You see a speed sign showing '70' as you leave a 50 zone.

subquestions.text: The new maximum from that sign is 70 km/h.
subquestions.explanation: A posted number sets the new maximum from the sign onward.

questions.scenario: Traffic ahead is heavy and moving slower than the limit.

subquestions.text: You must not exceed the limit, but you should also match the safe flow of traffic.
subquestions.explanation: The limit is a ceiling; driving far faster than surrounding traffic is unsafe.

questions.scenario: You are approaching roadworks with a temporary reduced speed limit sign.

subquestions.text: Temporary limits at roadworks are legally binding.
subquestions.explanation: Temporary signs override the normal limit for the marked stretch.

subquestions.text: You can ignore temporary limits if no workers are visible.
subquestions.explanation: Temporary limits apply regardless of whether workers are currently present.

questions.scenario: You are driving where the road surface is covered in fallen leaves and it has rained.

subquestions.text: You should reduce speed because grip is reduced.
subquestions.explanation: Wet leaves reduce traction; slow down.

questions.scenario: You see an electronic sign showing a lower variable speed limit on a motorway.

subquestions.text: Variable electronic limits are binding just like fixed signs.
subquestions.explanation: Electronic gantry limits are legally enforceable.

questions.scenario: You are driving downhill on a long slope.

subquestions.text: You should use engine braking to help control speed.
subquestions.explanation: Engine braking prevents overheating brakes on long descents.

questions.scenario: You are approaching a solid centre line (unbroken line) on a two-way road with a slow vehicle ahead.

subquestions.text: You must not cross the solid line to overtake.
subquestions.explanation: A solid centre line prohibits crossing to overtake.

subquestions.text: You may overtake if the road ahead looks clear.
subquestions.explanation: The solid line is a legal prohibition irrespective of visibility.

questions.scenario: You want to overtake just before a pedestrian crossing where someone may cross.

subquestions.text: Overtaking immediately before a pedestrian crossing is prohibited.
subquestions.explanation: Overtaking just before crossings is banned because it hides pedestrians from following/overtaking drivers.

questions.scenario: You are being overtaken by another vehicle on a single carriageway.

subquestions.text: You must not increase your speed while being overtaken.
subquestions.explanation: Speeding up during an overtake endangers both drivers and is prohibited.

subquestions.text: You may move slightly right to help the overtaking driver.
subquestions.explanation: Keeping right where safe assists a legal overtake.

questions.scenario: You are approaching the crest of a hill where you cannot see oncoming traffic.

subquestions.text: You must not overtake where your view of the road ahead is obstructed.
subquestions.explanation: Overtaking requires a clear view of sufficient road ahead; blind crests forbid it.

questions.scenario: A cyclist is riding ahead of you on a narrow road and you wish to pass.

subquestions.text: You must leave sufficient lateral distance when passing the cyclist.
subquestions.explanation: A safe side clearance is required when overtaking cyclists.

subquestions.text: You may pass closely as long as you do not touch the cyclist.
subquestions.explanation: Close passing is dangerous and not permitted; adequate clearance is required.

questions.scenario: You are on a road with two lanes in your direction and want to overtake.

subquestions.text: You should overtake using the lane to the left, then return right when safe.
subquestions.explanation: Overtake on the left and move back to the right lane once clear.

questions.scenario: You are approaching a level railway crossing and the car ahead is slow.

subquestions.text: You must not overtake at or immediately before a railway crossing.
subquestions.explanation: Overtaking is prohibited at level crossings for safety.

questions.scenario: A vehicle ahead is signalling and positioned to turn left.

subquestions.text: You may pass it on the right if there is room and it is safe.
subquestions.explanation: A vehicle waiting to turn left can be passed on the right where space allows.

questions.scenario: You want to overtake a long lorry on a two-lane road.

subquestions.text: You need more distance and time than to overtake a car.
subquestions.explanation: Longer vehicles require significantly more clear road to overtake safely.

subquestions.text: Overtaking a lorry takes the same distance as overtaking a car.
subquestions.explanation: A lorry's length means you need markedly more clear distance.

questions.scenario: You have started to overtake but realise the gap is closing with oncoming traffic.

subquestions.text: You should abort by easing off and dropping back safely.
subquestions.explanation: If in doubt, abandon the overtake and return behind the vehicle.

questions.scenario: There is a broken centre line on your side and a solid line on the oncoming side.

subquestions.text: You may overtake when your side has the broken line and it is safe.
subquestions.explanation: You follow the line on your side; broken permits overtaking when safe.

questions.scenario: You want to stop your car within 5 metres before a pedestrian crossing.

subquestions.text: Stopping and parking is prohibited that close before a crossing.
subquestions.explanation: Stopping/parking within the minimum distance before a crossing is banned to preserve visibility.

questions.scenario: You park on a hill facing downward.

subquestions.text: You should turn the front wheels toward the kerb.
subquestions.explanation: Turning wheels toward the kerb prevents the car rolling into the road if the brake fails.

subquestions.text: Leaving it in neutral with the handbrake off is acceptable on a slope.
subquestions.explanation: A parked car must be secured against rolling — handbrake on and in gear.

questions.scenario: You stop your car at a bus stop marked with the bus-stop sign to quickly drop off a passenger.

subquestions.text: Parking at a bus stop is prohibited.
subquestions.explanation: Parking at marked bus stops is banned; brief passenger set-down rules are limited and situation-dependent.

questions.scenario: You want to park across the entrance to someone's driveway.

subquestions.text: Parking that blocks a driveway entrance is prohibited.
subquestions.explanation: Obstructing entrances/exits is not allowed.

questions.scenario: You stop on a road with a sign showing a red circle with a single diagonal red line (no parking).

subquestions.text: You may stop briefly to set down passengers but not park.
subquestions.explanation: A no-parking sign forbids parking but generally allows brief stopping for boarding/alighting.

subquestions.text: The sign means you cannot even stop momentarily.
subquestions.explanation: That is the no-stopping sign (two crossed diagonal lines), which is different.

questions.scenario: You park at night on a poorly lit road outside a built-up area.

subquestions.text: You may need to leave parking lights on so the car is visible.
subquestions.explanation: On unlit roads a parked car may need to show parking lights for visibility.

questions.scenario: You want to stop on a pedestrian crossing to wait in traffic.

subquestions.text: You must not stop on a pedestrian crossing.
subquestions.explanation: Stopping on a crossing blocks pedestrians and is prohibited.

questions.scenario: There is a solid yellow line along the kerb.

subquestions.text: A kerb marking can indicate that stopping or parking is restricted.
subquestions.explanation: Yellow kerb markings signal parking/stopping restrictions.

questions.scenario: You park in a marked disabled bay without a valid permit.

subquestions.text: Parking there without a permit is not allowed.
subquestions.explanation: Disabled bays require a valid permit.

questions.scenario: You park facing against the direction of traffic on a two-way road at night.

subquestions.text: Parking against the traffic direction can be restricted and reduces visibility of your reflectors.
subquestions.explanation: Correct orientation matters for visibility and legality.

questions.scenario: You want to stop within a junction to wait for someone.

subquestions.text: Stopping within or too close to a junction is prohibited.
subquestions.explanation: Stopping in/near junctions blocks sightlines and turns.

questions.scenario: You are turning right and a cyclist is going straight ahead in the cycle lane to your right.

subquestions.text: You must give way to the cyclist before turning across the cycle lane.
subquestions.explanation: Right-turning vehicles yield to cyclists continuing straight in the cycle lane.

subquestions.text: The cyclist must stop because cars are larger.
subquestions.explanation: Vehicle size confers no priority; the turning driver yields.

questions.scenario: Children are playing near the roadway on a residential street.

subquestions.text: You should reduce speed and be ready to stop suddenly.
subquestions.explanation: Children are unpredictable; extra caution and low speed are required.

questions.scenario: You approach a stopped bus with its hazard/indicator lights on at a bus stop, and passengers are around it.

subquestions.text: You should slow down and watch for pedestrians crossing.
subquestions.explanation: People may cross in front of or behind a stopped bus, so reduce speed and stay alert.

questions.scenario: An elderly pedestrian is crossing slowly and the light turns green for you.

subquestions.text: You must let them finish crossing before you move off.
subquestions.explanation: Pedestrians already crossing must be allowed to complete the crossing safely.

questions.scenario: You open your car door after parking on a street with cycle traffic.

subquestions.text: You must check for cyclists before opening the door.
subquestions.explanation: Door-checking prevents 'dooring' collisions with passing cyclists.

subquestions.text: Cyclists are responsible for avoiding opening doors, not the driver.
subquestions.explanation: The person opening the door must ensure it is safe to do so.

questions.scenario: You see a blind pedestrian with a white cane near a crossing.

subquestions.text: You should show extra caution and be ready to give way.
subquestions.explanation: Vulnerable pedestrians such as those with impaired sight require extra care.

questions.scenario: You are turning right where a cycle path crosses your path and cyclists may be approaching from behind on your right.

subquestions.text: You should check your right-side blind spot for cyclists before turning.
subquestions.explanation: Right-turn/cyclist conflicts are a major crash cause; check the blind spot.

questions.scenario: A ball rolls into the road from between parked cars in a residential area.

subquestions.text: You should slow immediately and expect a child may follow it.
subquestions.explanation: A ball often precedes a running child; anticipate and slow.

questions.scenario: You approach a group of horse riders on a rural road.

subquestions.text: You should slow down and pass wide and gently to avoid spooking the horses.
subquestions.explanation: Horses can be startled; pass slowly with plenty of room.

questions.scenario: A moped rider is ahead of you in a cycle lane where mopeds are permitted.

subquestions.text: You should treat the moped like other vulnerable users and keep distance.
subquestions.explanation: Small two-wheelers need extra space and care.

questions.scenario: A pedestrian steps out unexpectedly from behind a parked van.

subquestions.text: You should brake and be ready for hidden pedestrians near parked vehicles.
subquestions.explanation: Parked vehicles hide pedestrians; anticipate and slow.

questions.scenario: Children are getting off a school bus that has stopped ahead.

subquestions.text: You should slow right down and watch for children crossing.
subquestions.explanation: Children may cross unexpectedly around a stopped school bus.

questions.scenario: You are joining a motorway from an on-ramp (acceleration lane).

subquestions.text: You should adjust your speed to merge smoothly with traffic.
subquestions.explanation: Use the acceleration lane to match traffic speed before merging.

subquestions.text: Traffic on the motorway must brake to let you in.
subquestions.explanation: Merging traffic adapts to the flow; through-traffic is not obliged to brake.

questions.scenario: You want to stop on the hard shoulder because you are tired.

subquestions.text: Stopping on the hard shoulder is only permitted in an emergency.
subquestions.explanation: The hard shoulder is for breakdowns/emergencies, not rest — use a rest area instead.

questions.scenario: You are driving in the left (overtaking) lane after completing an overtake.

subquestions.text: You should return to the right lane when safe.
subquestions.explanation: Keep right except when overtaking; the left lane is not for continuous cruising.

questions.scenario: You miss your motorway exit.

subquestions.text: You should continue to the next exit rather than reverse or stop.
subquestions.explanation: Reversing or stopping on a motorway is dangerous and prohibited; carry on to the next exit.

subquestions.text: You may reverse carefully on the hard shoulder to reach the exit.
subquestions.explanation: Reversing on a motorway is never allowed.

questions.scenario: There is congestion ahead and traffic is slowing sharply on the motorway.

subquestions.text: Using hazard lights briefly can warn drivers behind of the sudden slowdown.
subquestions.explanation: Brief hazard-light use alerts following traffic to unexpected queues.

questions.scenario: You break down on the motorway and manage to reach the hard shoulder.

subquestions.text: You should leave the vehicle from the side away from traffic and stand behind the barrier.
subquestions.explanation: Exit away from live lanes and wait in a safe place behind the barrier.

questions.scenario: You are on a motorway and want to change lanes to the left to overtake.

subquestions.text: You should check mirrors and blind spot and signal before moving.
subquestions.explanation: Mirror-signal-blind spot sequence is required before any lane change.

questions.scenario: Traffic on the motorway is stopped and emergency vehicles need to pass.

subquestions.text: You should form an emergency corridor by moving toward the lane edges.
subquestions.explanation: Creating a rescue lane lets emergency vehicles through stopped traffic.

questions.scenario: You are driving on a motorway at night and a vehicle behind has very bright lights.

subquestions.text: You should avoid staring at the mirror and can dip the interior mirror.
subquestions.explanation: Reducing glare from behind (anti-dazzle mirror) keeps you safe.

questions.scenario: You want to leave the motorway at your exit.

subquestions.text: You should move into the deceleration lane before slowing down.
subquestions.explanation: Slow in the exit/deceleration lane, not on the main carriageway.

questions.scenario: A slower vehicle is ahead in your lane and the left lane is clear.

subquestions.text: You may move left to overtake, then return right.
subquestions.explanation: Overtake on the left and return to the right lane afterwards.

questions.scenario: Your car's tyres are worn close to the legal minimum tread depth.

subquestions.text: Worn tyres reduce grip, especially in wet conditions.
subquestions.explanation: Low tread reduces water dispersal and braking grip, raising aquaplaning risk.

subquestions.text: Tread depth has no effect on braking distance.
subquestions.explanation: Tread directly affects grip and braking distance.

questions.scenario: One of your brake lights is not working.

subquestions.text: You should repair it before driving, as following drivers cannot see when you brake.
subquestions.explanation: Functioning brake lights are a legal and safety requirement.

questions.scenario: It is dark and visibility is poor due to fog.

subquestions.text: You should use dipped headlights and fog lights if fitted.
subquestions.explanation: Dipped beams and fog lights improve visibility without dazzling others; full beam reflects off fog.

subquestions.text: Full beam headlights are best in fog.
subquestions.explanation: Full beam reflects off fog droplets and worsens visibility.

questions.scenario: Your windscreen washer fluid is empty and the windscreen is dirty.

subquestions.text: A dirty windscreen reduces visibility and should be cleaned before driving.
subquestions.explanation: Clear vision is required; washer fluid and wipers must be functional.

questions.scenario: Your car is heavily loaded with luggage affecting the headlight aim.

subquestions.text: You may need to adjust the headlight level so you do not dazzle oncoming drivers.
subquestions.explanation: Heavy rear loads tilt beams up; adjust the level control to avoid dazzling.

questions.scenario: You notice the brake warning light stays on while driving.

subquestions.text: You should investigate the brake system before continuing to drive.
subquestions.explanation: A persistent brake warning can indicate a safety-critical fault.

questions.scenario: Your tyres are significantly under-inflated.

subquestions.text: Under-inflation increases wear, fuel use, and the risk of a blowout.
subquestions.explanation: Low pressure harms handling, economy and tyre safety.

questions.scenario: A warning light for the engine (check engine) comes on steadily.

subquestions.text: You should have the cause checked; it may affect emissions or reliability.
subquestions.explanation: An engine warning should be diagnosed rather than ignored.

questions.scenario: Your load extends beyond the rear of the vehicle.

subquestions.text: An overhanging load may need to be marked so others can see it.
subquestions.explanation: Projecting loads must be marked for visibility and legality.

questions.scenario: Your rear window and mirrors are iced over on a winter morning.

subquestions.text: You must clear ice so you have full visibility before driving.
subquestions.explanation: Driving with obscured windows/mirrors is unsafe and not allowed.

questions.scenario: One headlight is much dimmer than the other at night.

subquestions.text: You should fix it so you can see and be seen properly.
subquestions.explanation: Working headlights are essential and legally required.

questions.scenario: You are waiting in a stationary queue that will not move for several minutes.

subquestions.text: Switching off the engine reduces fuel use and emissions.
subquestions.explanation: Idling wastes fuel and emits pollutants; turning off the engine when stopped for a while is greener.

questions.scenario: You accelerate hard and brake sharply frequently during a trip.

subquestions.text: Smooth acceleration and anticipation reduce fuel consumption.
subquestions.explanation: Gentle, anticipatory driving lowers fuel use and wear.

subquestions.text: Aggressive acceleration has no impact on fuel economy.
subquestions.explanation: Hard acceleration significantly increases fuel consumption.

questions.scenario: You are driving and change gear at the right engine revs.

subquestions.text: Shifting up early at lower revs generally saves fuel.
subquestions.explanation: Driving in higher gears at lower revs reduces fuel consumption.

questions.scenario: You carry a roof box you no longer need for several weeks.

subquestions.text: Removing unused roof boxes reduces drag and fuel use.
subquestions.explanation: Roof boxes increase aerodynamic drag and fuel consumption.

questions.scenario: You are approaching a red light you can see from a distance.

subquestions.text: Easing off early and coasting to the light saves fuel versus braking late.
subquestions.explanation: Anticipating stops and coasting reduces fuel use and brake wear.

questions.scenario: You make many short cold-start trips each day.

subquestions.text: Combining short trips reduces cold-engine fuel waste and emissions.
subquestions.explanation: Cold engines burn more fuel; combining trips is more efficient.

questions.scenario: You leave the engine idling to warm up for several minutes before setting off in winter.

subquestions.text: Modern engines are best warmed by gentle driving, not long idling.
subquestions.explanation: Long idling wastes fuel; drive off gently to warm up.

questions.scenario: You arrive first at a road accident with injured people.

subquestions.text: You should secure the scene and warn other traffic before helping.
subquestions.explanation: Securing the scene (hazard lights, warning triangle) prevents further collisions.

subquestions.text: You should immediately move all injured people off the road.
subquestions.explanation: Injured persons should generally not be moved unless in immediate danger, to avoid worsening injuries.

questions.scenario: An injured person is unconscious but breathing.

subquestions.text: Placing them in the recovery position helps keep the airway clear.
subquestions.explanation: The recovery position keeps the airway open and reduces choking risk.

questions.scenario: A casualty is bleeding heavily from a limb.

subquestions.text: Applying firm pressure to the wound helps control bleeding.
subquestions.explanation: Direct pressure is a primary method to limit heavy bleeding.

questions.scenario: You need to call emergency services at an accident in Denmark.

subquestions.text: The emergency number to call is 112.
subquestions.explanation: 112 is the emergency number in Denmark and across the EU.

questions.scenario: A casualty is not breathing normally after an accident.

subquestions.text: You should call 112 and begin CPR if trained.
subquestions.explanation: Absent normal breathing calls for emergency services and CPR.

questions.scenario: There is a fuel leak and risk of fire at the accident scene.

subquestions.text: You should keep bystanders back and avoid ignition sources.
subquestions.explanation: Fuel leaks are a fire risk; keep the area clear of sparks and flames.

questions.scenario: Someone at the scene is in shock, pale and cold.

subquestions.text: You should keep them warm and reassured while waiting for help.
subquestions.explanation: Managing shock involves warmth, reassurance and monitoring.

categories.category: Alcohol, drugs & fitness to drive (Spirituskørsel og køreegnethed)

questions.scenario: You had several alcoholic drinks and feel fine to drive.

subquestions.text: Alcohol impairs reaction time and judgement even when you feel fine.
subquestions.explanation: Impairment occurs before subjective feelings of drunkenness; perceived readiness is unreliable.

subquestions.text: Coffee will make you safe to drive quickly after drinking.
subquestions.explanation: Only time lowers blood alcohol; caffeine does not remove impairment.

questions.scenario: You are very tired after a long day and consider a long night drive.

subquestions.text: Fatigue impairs driving similarly to alcohol and increases crash risk.
subquestions.explanation: Drowsiness slows reactions and attention; rest before driving.

questions.scenario: You are taking prescription medication that causes drowsiness.

subquestions.text: Some medicines can impair driving and you should check warnings.
subquestions.explanation: Certain medications affect alertness and reaction time; heed the warnings.

questions.scenario: You drank alcohol last night and are driving early the next morning.

subquestions.text: Alcohol may still be in your system and impair you the next morning.
subquestions.explanation: Alcohol clears slowly; you can still be over the limit hours later.

questions.scenario: You feel your eyelids getting heavy on a long drive.

subquestions.text: You should stop and rest rather than push on.
subquestions.explanation: Microsleeps are dangerous; rest before continuing.

questions.scenario: A friend offers you a lift after they've been drinking.

subquestions.text: You should decline and find a sober driver or other transport.
subquestions.explanation: Never ride with an impaired driver; arrange a safe alternative.

questions.scenario: You wear glasses for driving but left them at home.

subquestions.text: You should not drive if a vision correction condition on your licence isn't met.
subquestions.explanation: You must meet any eyesight conditions attached to your licence.

questions.scenario: You are driving and get stopped by police for a check.

subquestions.text: You must be able to identify yourself and show you are entitled to drive.
subquestions.explanation: Drivers must be able to establish identity and driving entitlement on request.

questions.scenario: Your car is required to have valid third-party liability insurance.

subquestions.text: Driving without mandatory liability insurance is illegal.
subquestions.explanation: Mandatory liability insurance is a legal requirement for operating a vehicle.

questions.scenario: You have modified or replaced key details of your vehicle.

subquestions.text: Significant changes may need to be registered with authorities.
subquestions.explanation: Certain vehicle changes require re-registration or approval.

questions.scenario: You lend your car to a friend who is not insured to drive it.

subquestions.text: The driver must be covered by valid insurance to drive legally.
subquestions.explanation: Driving without valid insurance cover is illegal.

questions.scenario: You are involved in a minor collision with another car.

subquestions.text: You should exchange details with the other driver.
subquestions.explanation: Exchanging identity and insurance details is required after a collision.

questions.scenario: Your vehicle inspection (syn) is overdue.

subquestions.text: Driving with an overdue mandatory inspection can be an offence.
subquestions.explanation: Vehicles must have a valid periodic inspection where required.

questions.scenario: You are driving abroad within the EU with your Danish licence.

subquestions.text: A valid Danish/EU licence is generally recognised across the EU.
subquestions.explanation: EU driving licences are mutually recognised within the EU.

questions.scenario: You see a triangular sign with a red border showing two children.

subquestions.text: It warns that children may be present, e.g. near a school.
subquestions.explanation: This warning sign flags likely child pedestrians ahead.

questions.scenario: You see a round sign with a red border and a white horizontal bar (no entry).

subquestions.text: It means you must not enter in that direction.
subquestions.explanation: The no-entry sign prohibits entry from that direction.

questions.scenario: You see a round blue sign showing a bicycle.

subquestions.text: It marks a compulsory cycle path for cyclists.
subquestions.explanation: Blue round signs give mandatory instructions; this designates a cycle path.

questions.scenario: You see a triangular sign showing a car skidding on a wet surface.

subquestions.text: It warns of a slippery road ahead.
subquestions.explanation: This warning sign indicates a risk of a slippery surface.

questions.scenario: You see a rectangular blue sign with a white 'P'.

subquestions.text: It indicates a parking area.
subquestions.explanation: The blue 'P' sign marks permitted parking.

questions.scenario: You see a triangular sign showing a roundabout symbol.

subquestions.text: It warns that a roundabout is ahead.
subquestions.explanation: This warning sign indicates an approaching roundabout.

questions.scenario: You see a round red-bordered sign with a number and 't' (weight limit).

subquestions.text: It restricts vehicles above the stated weight.
subquestions.explanation: Weight-limit signs prohibit vehicles exceeding the figure shown.

questions.scenario: You see a rectangular sign with a white arrow on blue indicating a one-way street.

subquestions.text: Traffic flows only in the direction of the arrow.
subquestions.explanation: One-way signs permit travel in the indicated direction only.

questions.scenario: You see a triangular sign with a red border showing a pedestrian.

subquestions.text: It warns of a pedestrian crossing or pedestrians ahead.
subquestions.explanation: This warning sign flags likely pedestrians ahead.

categories.category: Category C — Vehicle dimensions & weight (Mål og vægt)

questions.scenario: You are driving a large lorry (Category C vehicle) approaching a bridge with a posted height limit lower than your vehicle.

subquestions.text: You must not pass under the bridge and should find an alternative route.
subquestions.explanation: Exceeding a posted height limit risks a serious collision with the structure; take another route.

subquestions.text: You may pass slowly if you think there is probably enough room.
subquestions.explanation: Guessing clearance is never acceptable; the posted limit is binding.

questions.scenario: Your lorry is loaded close to its maximum permitted total weight.

subquestions.text: Braking distance is longer than for a lighter or empty vehicle.
subquestions.explanation: Greater mass increases stopping distance significantly; leave more room.

subquestions.text: A fully loaded lorry stops in the same distance as an empty one.
subquestions.explanation: Heavier loads mean longer braking distances.

questions.scenario: You need to distribute cargo in the load area of your lorry.

subquestions.text: Load should be secured and distributed so it does not shift or overload an axle.
subquestions.explanation: Proper load distribution and securing prevents instability and axle overload.

questions.scenario: A weight limit sign on a road shows a figure below your lorry's total weight.

subquestions.text: You must not use that road with your vehicle.
subquestions.explanation: Weight-limit signs legally prohibit vehicles above the stated figure.

categories.category: Category C — Load securing (Fastgørelse af gods)

questions.scenario: You are carrying heavy steel pipes on a flatbed.

subquestions.text: The load must be secured against sliding, rolling and tipping.
subquestions.explanation: Loads must be restrained in all directions to prevent movement in transit.

questions.scenario: You notice one of your load straps is frayed and worn.

subquestions.text: You should replace it before relying on it to secure a load.
subquestions.explanation: Damaged securing equipment can fail; replace it before use.

questions.scenario: Your cargo is lighter than the vehicle's capacity but tall and narrow.

subquestions.text: A high centre of gravity increases the risk of tipping in bends.
subquestions.explanation: Tall loads raise the centre of gravity and reduce stability in corners.

subquestions.text: Only heavy loads affect stability, not tall ones.
subquestions.explanation: Height and centre of gravity matter as much as weight for stability.

questions.scenario: You are unsure whether your load exceeds the vehicle's rated axle loads.

subquestions.text: You should check axle loads, as overloading an axle is an offence and unsafe.
subquestions.explanation: Axle load limits must be respected, not just total weight.

categories.category: Category C — Driving & rest times (Køre- og hviletid)

questions.scenario: You have been driving a lorry for several hours and are approaching the legal daily driving limit.

subquestions.text: You must take the required breaks and rest periods set by the rules.
subquestions.explanation: Professional driving-time rules require breaks and daily/weekly rest to prevent fatigue.

subquestions.text: You can keep driving as long as you feel alert.
subquestions.explanation: Rest rules are mandatory regardless of how alert you feel.

questions.scenario: Your vehicle is fitted with a tachograph.

subquestions.text: The tachograph records driving time and must be used correctly.
subquestions.explanation: Tachographs log driving/rest time and must be operated as required by law.

questions.scenario: You feel drowsy but are close to your destination.

subquestions.text: You should stop and rest rather than risk driving a large vehicle while tired.
subquestions.explanation: Fatigue in a heavy vehicle is especially dangerous; rest before continuing.

questions.scenario: You are turning right at a junction in a long lorry.

subquestions.text: You must account for the rear wheels cutting in (off-tracking) toward the kerb.
subquestions.explanation: Long vehicles' rear wheels follow a tighter path; watch for cyclists and the kerb.

subquestions.text: A lorry turns exactly like a car with no extra room needed.
subquestions.explanation: Long vehicles need extra room and swing differently when turning.

questions.scenario: You are reversing a large vehicle where your mirrors leave blind areas.

subquestions.text: You should use a banksman/observer or get out and check if unsure.
subquestions.explanation: Large blind zones when reversing call for extra checks or a spotter.

questions.scenario: You are driving a high-sided lorry in strong crosswinds.

subquestions.text: You should reduce speed and grip the wheel firmly as wind can push the vehicle.
subquestions.explanation: High-sided vehicles are strongly affected by crosswinds; slow and stay alert.

questions.scenario: You approach a steep downhill gradient with a loaded lorry.

subquestions.text: You should select a lower gear and use engine braking to avoid overheating the brakes.
subquestions.explanation: Engine braking on descents prevents brake fade in heavy vehicles.

questions.scenario: You are about to set off and perform a walk-around check of the lorry.

subquestions.text: Daily checks of tyres, lights, brakes and load are part of a driver's responsibility.
subquestions.explanation: Pre-drive checks on a commercial vehicle are a core safety duty.

questions.scenario: You discover a defect that affects the lorry's roadworthiness before a trip.

subquestions.text: You should not drive until the defect is properly addressed.
subquestions.explanation: Driving a large vehicle with a safety-critical defect is unsafe and unlawful.

questions.scenario: Your lorry emits visible black smoke and may exceed emissions rules.

subquestions.text: You should have it checked, as commercial vehicles must meet emissions standards.
subquestions.explanation: Excess emissions can breach standards and indicate a fault needing attention.
